title: Chapter 95 — The Cassock
paragraphs: Had you stepped aboard the Pequod at a certain point in this post-mortem of the whale and strolled forward near the windlass, I am quite sure you would have studied with no small curiosity a very strange, puzzling object lying lengthwise in the lee scuppers. Not the wondrous cistern in the whale's huge head; not the wonder of his unhinged lower jaw; not the miracle of his symmetrical tail — none of these would so surprise you as half a glimpse of that unaccountable cone, longer than a Kentuckian is tall, nearly a foot in diameter at the base, and jet-black as Yojo, the ebony idol of Queequeg. And an idol, indeed, it is — or rather, in old times, its likeness was. Such an idol as that found in the secret groves of Queen Maachah in Judea, and for worshipping which King Asa, her son, deposed her, destroyed the idol, and burnt it as an abomination at the brook Kedron, as darkly set forth in the fifteenth chapter of the First Book of Kings.

Look at the sailor called the mincer, who now comes along and, assisted by two helpers, heavily shoulders the grandissimus, as the mariners call it, and with bowed shoulders staggers off with it as if he were a soldier carrying a dead comrade from the field. Laying it upon the forecastle deck, he proceeds to remove its dark skin cylindrically, as an African hunter skins a boa. This done, he turns the skin inside out like a trouser leg, gives it a good stretching so as almost to double its diameter, and at last hangs it, well spread, in the rigging to dry. Before long it is taken down. Removing some three feet from the pointed end and then cutting two slits for armholes at the other end, he lengthwise slips himself bodily into it. The mincer now stands before you invested in the full ceremonial garments of his calling. From time immemorial to all his order, this investiture alone will adequately protect him while employed in the peculiar functions of his office.

That office consists in mincing the horse-pieces of blubber for the pots — an operation conducted at a curious wooden horse planted endwise against the bulwarks, with a capacious tub beneath it into which the minced pieces drop, fast as the sheets from a hurried speaker's desk. Arrayed in decent black, occupying a conspicuous pulpit, intent on Bible leaves — what a candidate for an archbishop, what a lad for a Pope, this mincer!*

*Bible leaves! Bible leaves! This is the invariable cry from the mates to the mincer. It commands him to be careful and cut his work into the thinnest possible slices, inasmuch as by doing so the business of boiling out the oil is much accelerated and its quantity considerably increased, besides perhaps improving it in quality.
